2.summary: A VLAN is a logical grouping of network devices into a single broadcast domain, or flat network.
2.deeper: A flat network has one broadcast domain: every connected device sees every broadcast packet. As network-intensive applications grow, that traffic causes bandwidth problems. Switches use VLANs to split the network into smaller broadcast domains, so a broadcast from one VLAN does not reach another. Because of this split, communication between VLANs must go through a Layer 3 routing process.
2.analogy: Think of one large open office where anyone who speaks up is heard by everyone. VLANs put up walls so each team hears only its own announcements. To pass a message to another team, someone has to carry it through the door; in the network, that door is the Layer 3 routing process.
2.scenario: An airman sees bandwidth problems on a network where thousands of computers send broadcast hello packets that every computer sees. Grouping the devices into VLANs keeps each broadcast inside its own VLAN. Two computers in different VLANs can still communicate, but only through a Layer 3 routing process.
2.example: In a school, an announcement over one shared intercom reaches every classroom, even rooms that do not need it. A VLAN works like giving each group its own intercom channel, so an announcement reaches only that group. In the course: a VLAN is a “logical” grouping of network devices into a single broadcast domain or flat network, Block Text p.15.

questions.stem: What is a VLAN?

answers.text: A logical grouping of network devices into a single broadcast domain
answers.why: This is the definition: a VLAN is a “logical” grouping of network devices into a single broadcast domain or flat network.

answers.text: A Layer 3 routing process that joins two broadcast domains
answers.why: Routing is what traffic needs to move between VLANs. The VLAN is the grouping of devices, not the routing process.

answers.text: A broadcast hello packet that a computer sends to every device
answers.why: The hello packet is an example of a broadcast that VLANs limit. It is not the VLAN itself.

answers.text: The forward or filter decision a switch makes for each frame
answers.why: The forward or filter decision is something switches already do. VLANs are something else switches can do to keep traffic local.

questions.hint: Think about what a VLAN groups together, and what each group shares.
questions.takeaway: A VLAN is a logical group of devices that shares one broadcast domain.

questions.stem: A Sales computer in VLAN 10 sends data to a Research computer in VLAN 30. Tap the part of the picture that lets the traffic cross from one VLAN to the other.

answers.text: VLAN 10 Sales
answers.why: The Sales VLAN is where the traffic starts. A VLAN keeps its traffic inside its own broadcast domain, so it cannot pass the traffic to another VLAN.

answers.text: VLAN 30 Research
answers.why: The Research VLAN is where the traffic must arrive. Its own broadcast domain does not reach VLAN 10.

answers.text: Layer 3 Routing
answers.why: Because VLANs segment the network, communication between VLANs must go through a Layer 3 routing process.

answers.text: Switch
answers.why: The switch uses VLANs to keep a broadcast from one VLAN from going to another VLAN. By itself, it keeps the VLANs apart.

questions.takeaway: Traffic between two VLANs must go through a Layer 3 routing process.

2.summary: A flat network has a single broadcast domain: every connected device sees every broadcast packet that is transmitted.
2.deeper: In a small network this is not a problem. When thousands of computers each send a broadcast hello packet that all connected computers see, bandwidth issues start. Switches provide limited Layer 3 services (broadcast control) by using VLANs to create smaller broadcast domains, so a broadcast from one VLAN does not go to another.
2.analogy: A broadcast domain is like the reach of one building alarm: everyone in the building hears it, whether it concerns them or not. Smaller broadcast domains are like separate alarms for separate buildings.
2.scenario: On a flat network, an airman counts thousands of computers, each sending a broadcast hello packet. Every connected computer sees every one of those packets, and the network starts to have bandwidth issues. The answer is to use VLANs to break the one broadcast domain into smaller ones.
2.example: In a group text with the whole neighborhood, every message reaches every phone in the group, even when it is meant for one house. That shared reach is like one broadcast domain. In the course: flat networks have a single broadcast domain, meaning that every connected device sees every broadcast packet that is transmitted, Block Text p.15.

answers.text: Every connected device

2.summary: Increased security is a VLAN benefit: only devices in the same VLAN receive a frame, so traffic from one VLAN is not accessible from another.
2.deeper: Every broadcast frame sent on a segment is seen by all devices on that segment, whether or not they need the data. With VLANs, only devices in the same VLAN receive the frame. The administrator controls each port and the resources it is allowed to use, and VLANs keep local traffic local to its broadcast domain.
2.analogy: It is like mail sorted into locked mailboxes by team: a letter for one team goes only into that team's box, and the other teams cannot read it.
2.scenario: Sales and Research share one switch. Before VLANs, every broadcast frame from Sales reached the Research devices too. After the airman puts Sales in VLAN 10 and Research in VLAN 30, a Sales frame reaches only the VLAN 10 devices, and Research cannot access that traffic.
2.example: In an apartment building, a note slipped under one door is read by that household only, while a note pinned up in the lobby is seen by everyone who walks by. VLANs move traffic from the lobby to behind the right door. In the course: security is increased because only those devices part of the same VLAN will receive the frame, Block Text p.16.

picture.alt: A frame from a Sales computer reaches every device on a flat segment, then only Sales devices once VLANs are used.

steps.caption: Without VLANs, every broadcast frame on a segment is seen by all devices, whether they need the data or not.
With VLANs, only devices in the same VLAN receive the frame.
Traffic from one VLAN is not accessible from another: Research does not see the Sales frame.
The administrator controls each port and whatever resources it is allowed to use.

questions.stem: Why do VLANs increase security?

answers.text: Every device on the segment sees every broadcast frame
answers.why: That is the problem VLANs address. Without VLANs, every broadcast frame on a segment is seen by all devices, whether they need the data or not.

answers.text: Unused ports stay active in default VLAN 1
answers.why: The opposite is true: any port that is not used should be shut down and assigned to an inactive VLAN to reduce vulnerabilities and improve security.

answers.text: Devices are grouped by their physical location
answers.why: With VLANs you are no longer confined to creating workgroups based on physical locations.

answers.text: Only devices in the same VLAN receive the frame
answers.why: Security is increased because only those devices part of the same VLAN will receive the frame.

questions.hint: Compare who receives a frame without VLANs and with them.
questions.takeaway: With VLANs, a frame reaches only the devices in its own VLAN.

choices.why: In one broadcast domain, every broadcast frame is seen by all devices on the segment, whether they need the data or not.

questions.takeaway: VLANs increase security because only devices in the same VLAN receive a frame, and the administrator controls each port.

2.summary: Cisco switches come with default VLAN 1 already created, and every switch port starts in VLAN 1 until the administrator changes it.
2.deeper: After you create more VLANs, you assign selected switch ports to each one. Ports you do not move stay in VLAN 1; in the show vlan output (Figure 2-2), every port except Fa0/1, Fa0/2 and Fa0/3 is still in default VLAN 1. Any port that is not used should be shut down and assigned to an inactive VLAN to reduce vulnerabilities and improve security.
2.analogy: Default VLAN 1 is like the lobby of a new office building: every new arrival waits there until someone assigns them to an office.
2.scenario: MSgt Rush runs show vlan on a switch where VLANs 10, 20 and 30 were just created. Ports Fa0/1, Fa0/2 and Fa0/3 are members of their VLANs; all the other ports still show under VLAN 1, because no one has moved them yet.
2.example: On a new phone, every app sits on the home screen until you move it into a folder. Switch ports start the same way, all in one default group. In the course: initially, all switch ports are assigned to default VLAN 1 until changed by the administrator, Block Text p.17.

picture.alt: A Cisco switch with four computers on ports Fa0/1 to Fa0/4: all start in default VLAN 1; three are moved to VLANs 10, 20 and 30; Fa0/4 stays in VLAN 1, as the show vlan output lists.

All the other ports are still assigned to default VLAN 1, as the show vlan output lists.
A port that is not used should be shut down and assigned to an inactive VLAN to reduce vulnerabilities.

2.summary: A VLAN membership shows which VLAN is assigned to a physical switch port for traffic forwarding and filtering.
2.deeper: A port can only be a member of one VLAN. On Cisco switches, you view memberships with the show vlan command in privileged EXEC mode. In Figure 2-2, ports Fa0/1, Fa0/2 and Fa0/3 are members of VLANs 10 (Sales), 20 (Marketing) and 30 (Research); all the other ports are still in default VLAN 1.
2.analogy: Port membership is like a seat on a team roster: each seat belongs to one team, and the roster lists who sits where.
2.scenario: An airman is asked which VLAN port Fa0/2 forwards traffic for. The airman runs show vlan in privileged EXEC mode and finds Fa0/2 listed under VLAN 20, Marketing.
2.example: In a school, each student is listed on the roster of one homeroom. A switch port's membership works like that roster entry: it says which group the port belongs to. In the course: a VLAN membership indicates which VLAN or VLANs are assigned to a certain physical port for traffic forwarding and filtering, Block Text p.17.

2.summary: A trunk is a connection between network devices that can carry more than one VLAN.
2.deeper: When an Ethernet frame crosses a trunk, a VLAN tag is applied so the switches can keep track of which VLAN each frame belongs to. In Figure 2-3, Sales is tag 10, Marketing is tag 20 and Research is tag 30. Trunks are also known as tagged ports; access ports, which are members of only one VLAN, are also known as untagged ports.
2.analogy: A trunk is like a highway between two cities that carries trucks from many companies. Each truck carries its company's label, so it is sent to the right depot at the other end.
2.scenario: An airman connects an access switch to a distribution switch. Sales, Marketing and Research traffic all has to cross that one connection, so it is set up as a trunk. Each frame that crosses it carries its VLAN tag: 10, 20 or 30.
2.example: A shared school hallway carries students from every class at once, but each student wears a class badge, so they end up in the right room. A trunk carries many VLANs over one connection in the same way. In the course: a trunk is a connection between network devices that can carry more than one VLAN, Block Text p.18.

picture.alt: Two switches joined by a trunk that carries Sales and Research frames, each with its VLAN tag.

steps.caption: A trunk is a connection between network devices that can carry more than one VLAN.
A Sales frame crosses the trunk with VLAN tag 10.
A Research frame crosses the same trunk with VLAN tag 30.
Trunks are also known as tagged ports; access ports, members of only one VLAN, are untagged ports.

answers.text: A trunk is a member of only one VLAN
answers.why: Being a member of only one VLAN describes an access port, not a trunk.

answers.text: A trunk can carry more than one VLAN
answers.why: A trunk is a connection between network devices that can carry more than one VLAN.

answers.text: A trunk removes the VLAN tag from each frame
answers.why: The tag is removed when the frame is placed on an access port. On a trunk, a VLAN tag is applied.

answers.text: A trunk is also known as an untagged port
answers.why: Access ports are known as untagged ports. Trunks are known as tagged ports.

2.summary: Frame tagging (frame identification or encapsulation) assigns a user-defined trunking ID to each frame, matching the frame to its VLAN.
2.deeper: The switch examines this frame identifier to determine the frame's VLAN destination. The tag is applied when an Ethernet frame crosses a trunk, and it is used to keep track of frames traversing a switch fabric. When the frame is placed on an access port, the tag is removed.
2.analogy: A frame tag is like a luggage tag at an airport: the bag rides shared belts with many others, and the tag tells each handler where it goes. Once the bag reaches its owner, the tag has done its job.
2.scenario: A Research frame leaves one switch on a trunk carrying tag 30. The next switch reads tag 30, sends the frame toward the Research VLAN, and removes the tag when it places the frame on the access port of a Research computer.
2.example: At a coat check, each coat gets a numbered ticket, so it can hang on a shared rack and still go back to the right person. A VLAN tag does that job for a frame. In the course: frame tagging uniquely assigns a user-defined trunking ID to each frame, and the trunking ID matches the VLAN to the traffic belonging to that VLAN, Block Text p.18.

picture.alt: A Research frame gets tag 30 on the trunk, the next switch reads the tag, and the tag is removed at the access port.

steps.caption: A Research computer sends a frame to its switch.
When the frame crosses the trunk, a VLAN tag is applied: tag 30 for Research.
The next switch examines the tag to determine the frame's VLAN destination.
When the frame is placed on an access port, the tag is removed.

questions.stem: What does a switch use a frame's VLAN tag for?

answers.text: To determine the frame's VLAN destination
answers.why: The switch examines this frame identifier to determine the frame's VLAN destination.

answers.text: To send the frame to every VLAN
answers.why: The tag matches the frame to one VLAN; the switch uses it to find that VLAN destination, not to send the frame everywhere.

answers.text: To decide which unused ports to shut down
answers.why: Shutting down unused ports is an administrator's security step. The tag identifies the frame's VLAN.

answers.text: To give the switch an IP address for remote access
answers.why: The switch's IP address comes from the management VLAN configuration. The tag identifies the frame's VLAN.

questions.hint: The next switch reads the tag and then decides something about the frame.
questions.takeaway: The tag tells the switch the frame's VLAN destination.

questions.stem: A Research frame goes from a computer on Switch 1 to a Research computer on Switch 2. Put what happens to the frame in order.

steps.text: The tag is removed as the frame is placed on an access port.

steps.text: A VLAN tag is applied as the frame crosses the trunk.
steps.why: When an Ethernet frame crosses a trunk, a VLAN tag is applied: tag 30 for Research.

steps.text: The Research computer sends the frame to Switch 1 with no VLAN tag.
steps.why: Access ports are untagged ports, so the frame enters the switch without a tag.

steps.text: Switch 2 examines the tag to find the frame's VLAN destination.
steps.why: The switch examines the frame identifier to determine the frame's VLAN destination.

questions.takeaway: The tag is applied for the trunk, read by the next switch and removed at the access port.

2.summary: An access port is a port that is a member of only one VLAN; the VLAN tag is removed when a frame is placed on it.
2.deeper: Access ports are also known as untagged ports, and trunks are known as tagged ports. Frames carry a VLAN tag while they cross a trunk, so the switches can match them to their VLAN. On the access port, the frame goes out without that tag.
2.analogy: An access port is like a private driveway off a shared street: only one household uses it, so the delivery no longer needs the street-sorting label once it pulls in.
2.scenario: An airman connects a Marketing computer to port Fa0/2, a member of VLAN 20 only. Frames for that computer arrive over the trunk with tag 20; the switch removes the tag when it places them on the access port.
2.example: A mail carrier sorts letters by route in the truck, but once a letter is in your own mailbox, no one needs the route label. An access port is the frame's own mailbox. In the course: an access port is a port that is a member of only one VLAN, and when the frame is placed on it, the tag is removed, Block Text p.18.

picture.alt: A Marketing frame crosses the trunk with tag 20 and leaves on an access port without its tag.

2.summary: Inter-Switch Link (ISL) is the Cisco proprietary standard for trunks; it is deprecated.
2.deeper: ISL tags the frame, but instead of using the frame as it is, it adds a new header and trailer to the existing frame. IEEE 802.1q, the open standard, uses a space in the standard frame header instead. ISL only works with Cisco devices, while IEEE 802.1q works with all major manufacturers' models. In the example configuration, ISL is set with the command switchport trunk encapsulation ISL.
2.analogy: ISL is like putting a letter inside a new, larger envelope with its own address and seal. IEEE 802.1q is like writing the sorting note in a spare box already printed on the original envelope.
2.scenario: MSgt Rush asks why a trunk between a Cisco switch and another manufacturer's switch should not use ISL. The airman answers: ISL only works with Cisco devices, while IEEE 802.1q works with all major manufacturers' models.
2.example: A gift card from one store works only in that store, while a general gift card works in many stores. ISL is like the one-store card: it works only with one manufacturer's devices. In the course: Inter-Switch Link (ISL) is the Cisco proprietary standard for trunks (deprecated), and ISL only works with Cisco devices, Block Text p.18.

picture.alt: Two Cisco switches trunk with ISL, which wraps the frame in a new header and trailer; a third maker's switch trunks with IEEE 802.1q, which puts the tag in the frame header.

steps.caption: ISL, the Cisco proprietary standard for trunks, tags the frames that cross a trunk between Cisco switches.
Instead of using the frame as it is, ISL adds a new header and trailer to the existing frame.
IEEE 802.1q, the open standard, uses a space in the standard frame header for the tag.
ISL is deprecated and only works with Cisco devices; IEEE 802.1q works with all major manufacturers' models.

answers.text: It adds a new header and trailer to the existing frame
answers.why: ISL tags the frame but, instead of using the frame as it is, adds a new header and trailer to the existing frame.

answers.text: It uses a space in the standard frame header

2.summary: A management VLAN carries management traffic such as telnet, SNMP and syslog.
2.deeper: Switches use VLAN 1 as the default VLAN for in-band management and for protocols such as STP, CDP, DTP, VTP and PAgP, all untagged traffic. VLAN 1 may unwisely span the entire network if it is not pruned, and if its scope is large enough, the risk of compromise can increase significantly. So you should not make VLAN 1 the management VLAN. Best practice is to prune unnecessary ports from VLAN 1 and the management VLAN, and to separate in-band management, device protocol and data traffic.
2.analogy: A management VLAN is like a staff-only corridor in a hospital: the people who run the building use it, apart from the public hallways.
2.scenario: An airman sets up switch management. The airman does not use VLAN 1: the example configuration creates interface vlan 99 with the description Management VLAN, gives it an IP address and enters no shutdown. That IP address is only for remote access to the switch, not for a particular port.
2.example: Many stores have a back office where managers check the registers, apart from the sales floor that customers use. A management VLAN keeps the work of running the network apart from regular traffic in a similar way. In the course: the management VLAN is used for purposes such as telnet, SNMP and syslog, Block Text p.19.

questions.stem: Why should VLAN 1 not be the management VLAN?

answers.text: VLAN 1 cannot carry untagged traffic
answers.why: The protocols switches run on VLAN 1 are all untagged traffic, so VLAN 1 does carry it.

answers.text: VLAN 1 may span the entire network if not pruned, which can increase the risk of compromise
answers.why: VLAN 1 may unwisely span the entire network if not appropriately pruned, and if its scope is large enough, the risk of compromise can increase significantly.

answers.text: VLAN 1 only works with Cisco devices
answers.why: Working only with Cisco devices describes ISL trunking, not VLAN 1.

answers.text: VLAN 1 is removed when other VLANs are created
answers.why: Ports stay in default VLAN 1 until the administrator moves them, so creating other VLANs does not remove it.

questions.hint: Think about how far VLAN 1 can reach when no ports are pruned from it.
questions.takeaway: Keep management off VLAN 1: unpruned, it can span the whole network and raise the risk of compromise.

choices.text: A separate management VLAN, such as VLAN 99

choices.text: Prune them from VLAN 1 and the management VLAN
choices.why: Best practice prunes unnecessary ports from gaining access to VLAN 1 as well as the management VLAN.
If VLAN 1 spans a large enough scope, the risk of compromise can increase significantly.
